title: Lookalike domains and homoglyph tricks
body_md:
## Reading URLs like a defender

A convincing phishing campaign is mostly about a convincing domain name. Attackers have three reliable patterns to make a fake domain look almost identical to a real one. Once you can name them, you can spot them on first glance.

### 1. Character substitution

Replace one letter with a visually similar one. The most common pairs:

- `paypal.com` → `paypa1.com` (lowercase L replaced by digit 1)
- `google.com` → `g00gle.com` (letter o replaced by digit 0)
- `microsoft.com` → `rnicrosoft.com` (letter m replaced by rn)

In most fonts at small sizes, a casual reader sees the brand name and stops there.

### 2. Punycode and homoglyphs

The Internet supports international characters in domain names. Cyrillic letters `а`, `е`, `о`, `р`, `с`, `у`, `х` look identical to Latin `a, e, o, p, c, y, x` in many fonts. A domain registered as `аpple.com` (where the first `а` is Cyrillic) is visually identical to `apple.com` but goes to a completely different place.

Modern browsers usually display these as their Punycode form (`xn--pple-43d.com`) to expose the trick — but not always, and not in every interface.

### 3. Subdomain framing

The trick relies on the fact that humans read left to right. The attacker buys a generic-looking domain like `verify-account.io` and constructs subdomains under it:

- `paypal.com.verify-account.io`
- `appleid.apple.com.security-check.net`
- `myaccount.google.com.login-flow.cc`

The registered domain is always the *last* two labels before the slash — `verify-account.io`, `security-check.net`, `login-flow.cc`. Everything before that is just labels the attacker invented.

## The reading rule

For any URL, *read right-to-left from the first slash until you hit the first dot, then one more dot back*. That's the registered domain. Everything else is decoration.

```
https://login.paypal.com.security-check.net/verify
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                  registered domain
```

With practice this becomes automatic. Tap or hover the link, read the registered domain, decide. The whole motion takes a second.

widget_config.question: Which of these URLs would safely take you to a real Microsoft login page?

choices.explanation: Correct. The registered domain is `microsoftonline.com`, which is Microsoft's legitimate login domain. Subdomains like `login.` are fine — what matters is the registered domain at the rightmost-but-one position.
The registered domain here is `login-secure.cc`. The `account.microsoft.com.` part is just a deceptive subdomain. Classic subdomain-framing trick.

The registered domain is `microsoft-online.com`, which is **not** Microsoft. Attackers register hyphenated lookalikes precisely because they read fast. Microsoft's real one is `microsoftonline.com` without the hyphen.
Look at the second character of the registered domain: `rn` (r + n), not `m`. At small sizes the two are visually identical. This is the character-substitution trick.

widget_config.hint: For each URL, find the registered domain by reading right-to-left until you've passed exactly one dot.
